Two worlds, drawn as soft regions that blend where they meet; the blend is the boundary. A block of work is covered by a tool when the tool covers every feature the block needs: within 2× of the best tool on this device for a measured feature, 4 of 5 for a rubric one (italic: the author's judgement). Same rule for every tool; a dashed block is one no tool covers on this device. A tool's shape is the rounded convex hull of the blocks it covers and never encloses a block it does not cover (where one hull would, the tool is drawn in two or more pieces). Arrays cross zero-copy between raptor and CuPy, PyTorch, NVIDIA Warp and NumPy today, not JAX. The tools are complementary; overlap is not a ranking.

  1. 1 Ensemble speed faster is better
  2. 2 Footprint and turnaround lower is better
  3. 3 Tensors and precision (qualitative)
  4. 4 One-sample authoring (qualitative)
  5. 5 Low-level control (qualitative)
  6. 6 Reach (qualitative)
Ensemble speed
How fast a batch of independent samples runs: uneven, regular, small and adaptive workloads.
Footprint and turnaround
What the work costs around the run: the memory it holds, the time to compile and the code to write.
Tensors and precision (qualitative)
Dense tensor maths, array-style code and half precision: where PyTorch and JAX lead.
One-sample authoring (qualitative)
Writing the code for one sample and getting derivatives of it.
Low-level control (qualitative)
How much of the execution you control from the tool's own language.
Reach (qualitative)
Where the tool fits in: your arrays, deployment outside Python and extension to new targets.

Every measured axis is the per-sample ensemble workload raptor is built for; dense tensor maths, training and half precision are the qualitative axes, where PyTorch and JAX lead. Outer is better; overlaps are complementary, not a ranking.

NVIDIA Warp gives you near-total control of every kernel, short of raw CUDA. raptor hands that control to the engine on purpose, so compaction and the launch shape are decided at run time; the two are different trade-offs, not a ranking.

How to read this radar

Each of the six majors is the plain mean of its minor axes (the detailed radar draws every minor), with equal weights and the same rule for every tool; a minor a tool has no reading on is left out of its mean and the major's marker is drawn hollow. Hover or tap a major to see its minors.

  • Ensemble speed: Uneven ensembles, Regular ensembles, Small jobs and Adaptive ODEs; measured.
  • Footprint and turnaround: Memory, Compile time and Code size; measured.
  • Tensors and precision: Tensor workloads, Array-style programming and Half precision and below; qualitative.
  • One-sample authoring: Single-thread abstraction and Differentiable kernels; qualitative.
  • Low-level control: A single axis, so nothing is averaged; qualitative.
  • Reach: Works with your arrays, Deploy outside Python and Extensibility; qualitative.

Each measured axis is stretched over its own best-to-worst range, so ring labels differ per axis (compile time: fixed, 0.1 s to 100 s; code size: at least 4x). Axes are grouped by theme, so read the axes, not the area.

Italic axes are the author's judgement, not measurements: hollow markers, a linear scale, and no marker where a tool has no reading. A hollow marker on a measured axis means a minor is missing or, for compile time, is the tool's simple-kernel time. The hover panel has each axis's full wording.

Tensors2 of 5
Built for per-sample kernels and ensembles; for dense tensor work it hands arrays to PyTorch or JAX zero-copy.		2 of 5
Compiles loops and NumPy-style code; dense linear algebra comes from the libraries it calls.		5 of 5 ✓
Array programs written once and compiled by XLA; batched linear algebra, convolutions and broadcasting are first-class.		5 of 5 ✓
Dense array maths is its home ground, with tuned libraries behind batched linear algebra, convolutions and broadcasting.		4 of 5 ✓
The reference API for dense array maths and broadcasting on the CPU, with tuned BLAS and LAPACK underneath.
Array style2 of 5
A per-sample kernel language by design: you write one step of one sample, and whole-array code is left to array libraries, with which raptor exchanges arrays zero-copy.		2 of 5
You mostly write loops over arrays; array expressions are secondary.		4 of 5 ✓
NumPy-style array expressions, but functional and traced rather than eager.		5 of 5 ✓
Eager tensor expressions are the programming model.		5 of 5 ✓
The whole-array expression is the programming model, evaluated eagerly; the right choice for array code on the CPU.
Half precision1 of 5
Not supported. raptor is scoped to FP32 and FP64 numerics; half-precision and tensor-core work belongs with PyTorch or JAX.		2 of 5
float16 arithmetic intrinsics in numba.cuda; no BF16/FP8 or tensor-core path.		5 of 5 ✓
FP16, BF16 and FP8 types, with XLA targeting tensor cores.		5 of 5 ✓
FP16, BF16 and FP8 types with tensor-core paths, including autocast.		2 of 5
float16 storage and arithmetic, but slow on the CPU and nothing below it.
Single-thread5 of 5 ✓
You write one step of one sample; hawk and eagle handle threads, launches, stopping and compaction.		3 of 5
A per-index body under prange or cuda.jit; indexing and launch are yours.		4 of 5 ✓
A per-sample function under vmap; early stopping becomes masking you write.		3 of 5
torch.func.vmap over a per-sample function; stopping and batching stay with you.		1 of 5
Whole-array code; there is no per-sample model.
Derivatives5 of 5 ✓
Every kernel written in hawk's own vocabulary carries generated forward- and reverse-mode derivatives, on GPU and CPU.		1 of 5
No automatic differentiation of its own.		5 of 5 ✓
Forward and reverse mode through grad, jvp and vjp, on GPU and CPU.		4 of 5 ✓
Autograd differentiates tensor programs; a custom kernel needs its backward written by hand.		1 of 5
No automatic differentiation of its own.
Control2 of 5
By design hawk and eagle decide threads, launches and scheduling, so compaction can adapt to uneven batches; for hand-tuned thread-level kernels, Warp or Numba is the right choice.		5 of 5 ✓
prange, explicit threads and typed loops; SIMD and memory layout are yours.		2 of 5
Plain JAX leaves threads, vectorisation and layout to XLA; Pallas control is aimed at the GPU.		2 of 5
Operators and a few custom-kernel hooks; launches are left to the framework.		2 of 5
Strides and memory layout are yours to choose; threads and SIMD are left to the libraries underneath.
Your arrays4 of 5 ✓
Zero-copy through DLPack with a certified matrix (CuPy, PyTorch, Warp and NumPy today, not JAX).		3 of 5
Reads NumPy arrays directly and exposes the CUDA array interface; wider exchange takes some glue.		4 of 5 ✓
DLPack exchange with other frameworks, mostly without copies.		4 of 5 ✓
DLPack and the array interface exchange tensors with other libraries, mostly without copies.		4 of 5 ✓
The array protocols everyone reads, on the host; device memory is out of its scope.
Deploy4 of 5 ✓
A compiled kernel runs from any program that can load its manifest; today eagle is the loader.		2 of 5
Ahead-of-time compilation exists in a limited form; most use stays inside Python.		4 of 5 ✓
Compiled XLA programs can be exported and run from other runtimes.		4 of 5 ✓
TorchScript, AOT export and a C++ runtime take models into non-Python programs.		1 of 5
A Python library; nothing is compiled into a separate artefact.
Extensibility3 of 5

An extension API for new types and targets, at a low level.		4 of 5 ✓
XLA and PJRT plugins add new hardware backends.		4 of 5 ✓

Two worlds, drawn as soft regions that blend where they meet; the blend is the boundary. A block of work is covered by a tool when the tool covers every feature the block needs: within 2× of the best tool on this device for a measured feature, 4 of 5 for a rubric one (italic: the author's judgement). Same rule for every tool; a dashed block is one no tool covers on this device. A tool's shape is the rounded convex hull of the blocks it covers and never encloses a block it does not cover (where one hull would, the tool is drawn in two or more pieces). Arrays cross zero-copy between raptor and CuPy, PyTorch, NVIDIA Warp and NumPy today, not JAX. The tools are complementary; overlap is not a ranking.

  1. 1 Ensemble speed faster is better
  2. 2 Footprint and turnaround lower is better
  3. 3 Tensors and precision (qualitative)
  4. 4 One-sample authoring (qualitative)
  5. 5 Low-level control (qualitative)
  6. 6 Reach (qualitative)
Ensemble speed
How fast a batch of independent samples runs: uneven, regular, small and adaptive workloads.
Footprint and turnaround
What the work costs around the run: the memory it holds, the time to compile and the code to write.
Tensors and precision (qualitative)
Dense tensor maths, array-style code and half precision: where PyTorch and JAX lead.
One-sample authoring (qualitative)
Writing the code for one sample and getting derivatives of it.
Low-level control (qualitative)
How much of the execution you control from the tool's own language.
Reach (qualitative)
Where the tool fits in: your arrays, deployment outside Python and extension to new targets.

Every measured axis is the per-sample ensemble workload raptor is built for; dense tensor maths, training and half precision are the qualitative axes, where PyTorch and JAX lead. Outer is better; overlaps are complementary, not a ranking.

NVIDIA Warp gives you near-total control of every kernel, short of raw CUDA. raptor hands that control to the engine on purpose, so compaction and the launch shape are decided at run time; the two are different trade-offs, not a ranking.

How to read this radar

Each of the six majors is the plain mean of its minor axes (the detailed radar draws every minor), with equal weights and the same rule for every tool; a minor a tool has no reading on is left out of its mean and the major's marker is drawn hollow. Hover or tap a major to see its minors.

  • Ensemble speed: Uneven ensembles, Regular ensembles, Small jobs and Adaptive ODEs; measured.
  • Footprint and turnaround: Memory, Compile time and Code size; measured.
  • Tensors and precision: Tensor workloads, Array-style programming and Half precision and below; qualitative.
  • One-sample authoring: Single-thread abstraction and Differentiable kernels; qualitative.
  • Low-level control: A single axis, so nothing is averaged; qualitative.
  • Reach: Works with your arrays, Deploy outside Python and Extensibility; qualitative.

Each measured axis is stretched over its own best-to-worst range, so ring labels differ per axis (compile time: fixed, 0.1 s to 100 s; code size: at least 4x). Axes are grouped by theme, so read the axes, not the area.

Italic axes are the author's judgement, not measurements: hollow markers, a linear scale, and no marker where a tool has no reading. A hollow marker on a measured axis means a minor is missing or, for compile time, is the tool's simple-kernel time. The hover panel has each axis's full wording.
